name: Fallibilism
statement: We can know things without certainty; any belief we hold could turn out to be mistaken.
statementAccent: without certainty; any belief we hold could turn out to be mistaken
meaning: Fallibilism is the epistemological view that beliefs, even those that count as knowledge, can be justified or rationally held without certainty, and could in principle turn out to be false. On this view, no belief is ever rationally supported in a conclusive, error-excluding way; knowledge is compatible with the possibility of error and does not require infallible, indubitable certainty. Fallibilism is offered as a middle path between two extremes: Cartesian foundationalism, which demanded certainty as the standard for knowledge, and radical skepticism, which concluded that, since almost nothing is certain, we know almost nothing. The fallibilist accepts that our justification is not conclusive but denies that this costs us knowledge, holding instead that we can genuinely know many things even though our grounds fall short of certainty and our beliefs remain in principle revisable. The term fallibilism was introduced by the American pragmatist Charles Sanders Peirce in the late nineteenth century, though the underlying idea is older; Peirce framed it as a response to foundationalism, memorably describing our knowledge as never absolute but always, as it were, swimming in a continuum of uncertainty and indeterminacy. Crucially, Peirce was not a skeptic: he held that inquiry is ongoing and self-correcting, converging in the long run toward truth. Fallibilism is closely tied to the scientific method and is the mainstream position in contemporary epistemology.
mechanism: Fallibilism works by separating two things that certainty-based epistemologies run together: having knowledge and having conclusive, error-proof justification. The fallibilist holds that justification comes in degrees and need never reach the point of excluding all possibility of error; a belief can be well supported, rationally held, and even count as knowledge while still being such that, were things different in ways one cannot rule out, it would be false. This dissolves the skeptic's leverage. Infallibilism holds that to know p one's justification must guarantee p's truth, and since such guarantees are almost never available, infallibilism collapses into skepticism. The fallibilist rejects the demand: knowledge requires good, truth-conducive grounds, not a guarantee, so the fact that error is always in principle possible does not by itself defeat knowledge. Applied to science, fallibilism yields the picture of theories as provisional and corrigible, held tentatively and open to revision as new evidence arrives, with every belief in principle subject to correction. Peirce added a dynamic, optimistic element: although any particular result may be mistaken, the ongoing, self-correcting practice of inquiry tends over the long run to weed out error and converge asymptotically on the truth, so fallibility is compatible with real progress. The mechanism, in short, is to lower the bar from certainty to fallible but genuine justification, blocking skepticism while respecting the corrigibility of all human knowledge.

examples.text: I can know the sun will rise tomorrow even though my justification does not conclusively exclude every possibility of error.
Scientific theories are held provisionally and remain open to revision in light of new evidence, a fallibilist stance.
Peirce described knowledge as never absolute but always swimming in a continuum of uncertainty and indeterminacy.

variants.name: Fallibilism about justification
variants.text: The claim that justification need not be conclusive, applying primarily to the grounds of belief.

variants.name: Fallible knowledge thesis
variants.text: The stronger claim that a fallibly justified true belief can nonetheless constitute genuine knowledge.

whyItMatters: Fallibilism is the mainstream position in contemporary epistemology and philosophy of science, and its importance lies in offering a stable middle ground between two unattractive extremes. Against the Cartesian demand that knowledge requires certainty, a demand that, taken seriously, hands victory to the skeptic since so little is truly certain, fallibilism holds that we can have real knowledge on fallible grounds. Against radical skepticism, it preserves the everyday and scientific conviction that we know a great deal. This makes fallibilism the natural epistemology of science, which advances precisely by treating its theories as provisional, testable, and open to revision rather than as final and certain, a stance connected to Popper's falsificationism and to the pragmatist tradition. Peirce, who named the doctrine, tied it to a hopeful picture of inquiry as self-correcting and truth-seeking over the long run, so that acknowledging our fallibility need not breed despair but can motivate continued investigation. Fallibilism also frames live debates, such as whether one can coherently say I know that p but I might be wrong. As the view that knowledge is possible without certainty, fallibilism underwrites both a sane response to skepticism and the self-correcting spirit of science.

working.text: hold that a belief can count as knowledge without conclusive, error-excluding justification.
deny that knowing requires a guarantee of truth, which would collapse into skepticism.
treat beliefs, including scientific theories, as provisional and revisable in light of new evidence.

limits: Fallibilism, though mainstream, faces genuine puzzles. The sharpest is the phenomenon of concessive knowledge attributions, sometimes called the fallibilist's dilemma: sentences like I know that p, but I might be wrong sound linguistically odd, even contradictory, yet fallibilism seems committed to their being sometimes true, which exposes a real tension between fallibilism and ordinary knowledge-talk. There is also unresolved debate about how much possibility of error is compatible with knowledge, since if too much is allowed the notion of knowledge threatens to become empty, while if too little is allowed fallibilism slides back toward the certainty it rejects. It matters, too, to distinguish fallibilism about justification, the claim that our grounds need not be conclusive, from the stronger fallible knowledge thesis, that a merely fallibly justified true belief really can be knowledge, which is where the central controversy lies. The connection to Popper's falsificationism, while real, should be credited to Popper-specific sources rather than assumed. So fallibilism robustly makes knowledge possible without certainty, understood as the mainstream but not untroubled view facing the puzzle of concessive knowledge attributions and the question of how much error knowledge can tolerate.
misreadings: Fallibilism is not skepticism; it holds that we do have knowledge, only without certainty, whereas skepticism denies knowledge. It is not the claim that all beliefs are equally uncertain or that anything goes, since it still requires good, truth-conducive justification and allows beliefs to be well or poorly supported. And Peirce, who named it, was no skeptic but held inquiry to be self-correcting and truth-convergent, so treating fallibilism as skepticism, as epistemic relativism, or as counsel of despair, misreads the mainstream view that knowledge is possible without certainty.
origin: The epistemological view, named by Charles Sanders Peirce in the late nineteenth century, that beliefs can count as knowledge without certainty and are always in principle revisable, offered as a middle path between certainty-demanding foundationalism and skepticism.
